claims.source: Following the first nβ-catenin activation at the 16-cell stage, Foxa.a, Foxd, Fgf9/16/20, cadherinII and βCD1 (β-catenin downstream gene 1) are induced in the NNE cells, with at least Foxd and Fgf9/16/20 being direct targets of the β-catenin/Tcf7 complex (Imai, 2003; Imai et al., 2002a, 2002b, 2002c; Kumano et al., 2006; Oda-Ishii et al., 2016; Rothbächer et al., 2007; Satou et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claims.claim: In β-catenin–inhibited embryos analysed at the 16-cell stage, Foxd and Fgf9/16/20 expression was lost.
claims.source: Consistent with a recent study (Oda-Ishii et al., 2016), we confirmed that in β-catenin–inhibited (β-catenin-MO injected) embryos analysed at the 16-cell stage, Foxd and Fgf/9/16/20 expression was lost (Figure 1b).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claims.claim: Foxa.a is expressed in the a-line anterior ectoderm lineages in a nβ-catenin-independent fashion.
claims.source: In addition to the mesendoderm lineages, Foxa.a is also expressed in the a-line anterior ectoderm lineages in a nβ-catenin-independent fashion (Figure 1b,c) (Lamy et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1b,c and citation to Lamy et al., 2006.

claims.claim: In β-catenin–inhibited embryos, Foxa.a expression persisted in NNE and a-lineage cells, probably due to transformation of vegetal cells into animal cells.
claims.source: In β-catenin–inhibited embryos, Foxa.a expression persisted in NNE and a-lineage cells, probably due to transformation of vegetal cells into animal cells that has been reported previously (Figure 1b) (Imai et al., 2000; Oda-Ishii et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental observation in Figure 1b and inference supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Ectopic stabilisation of nβ-catenin resulted in activation of Foxa.a, Foxd, and Fgf9/16/20 in ectoderm lineages at the 16-cell stage.
claims.source: Conversely, ectopic stabilisation of nβ-catenin resulted in activation of all three genes in ectoderm lineages at the 16-cell stage (Figure 1c).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1c using BIO treatment.

claims.claim: Foxd, Foxa.a and Fgf9/16/20 are transcriptional targets of nβ-catenin in vegetal cells.
claims.source: Thus, our results confirm that Foxd, Foxa.a and Fgf9/16/20 are transcriptional targets of nβ-catenin in vegetal cells, although Foxa.a also has a nβ-catenin-independent expression in a-line animal cells.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data showing loss of expression upon β-catenin inhibition and gain of expression upon β-catenin activation.

claims.claim: Foxa.a has been shown to be required for both NN lineage and endoderm gene expression.
claims.source: Consistent with this idea, Foxa.a has been shown to be required for both NN lineage and endoderm gene expression (Imai et al., 2006), with Foxd specifically required for NN lineage, but not endoderm fates, and Fgf9/16/20 contributing to notochord induction from the NN lineage (Imai et al., 2002a, 2002b; Yasuo and Hudson, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Imai et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Foxd is specifically required for NN lineage, but not endoderm fates.
claims.source: Consistent with this idea, Foxa.a has been shown to be required for both NN lineage and endoderm gene expression (Imai et al., 2006), with Foxd specifically required for NN lineage, but not endoderm fates, and Fgf9/16/20 contributing to notochord induction from the NN lineage (Imai et al., 2002a, 2002b; Yasuo and Hudson, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Imai et al., 2002a, 2002b and Yasuo and Hudson, 2007.

claims.claim: Fgf9/16/20 contributes to notochord induction from the NN lineage.
claims.source: Consistent with this idea, Foxa.a has been shown to be required for both NN lineage and endoderm gene expression (Imai et al., 2006), with Foxd specifically required for NN lineage, but not endoderm fates, and Fgf9/16/20 contributing to notochord induction from the NN lineage (Imai et al., 2002a, 2002b; Yasuo and Hudson, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Imai et al., 2002a, 2002b and Yasuo and Hudson, 2007.

claims.claim: Inhibiting any one of Foxa.a, Foxd, or Fgf9/16/20 prevented the correct initiation of gene expression in both NN (Zic-r.b) and E (Lhx3/4) lineages.
claims.source: However, we found that inhibiting any one of these factors prevented the correct initiation of gene expression in both NN (Zic-r.b) and E (Lhx3/4) lineages (Figure 2a, Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2a and Table 1.

claims.claim: Fgf9/16/20 is responsible for the broad activation of ERK at the 32-cell stage in most vegetal lineages, including NN and E lineages, as well as two neural lineages in the ectoderm.
claims.source: We confirmed that Fgf9/16/20 is responsible for the broad activation of ERK at the 32-cell stage in most vegetal lineages, including NN and E lineages, as well as two neural lineages in the ectoderm (Figure 2—figure supplement 1f).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1f.

claims.claim: Treatment of embryos from the 16-cell stage with the MEK inhibitor U0126 inhibits ERK1/2 activation.
claims.source: Treatment of embryos from the 16-cell stage with the MEK inhibitor U0126, also inhibits this ERK1/2 activation (Kim and Nishida, 2001; Picco et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Kim and Nishida, 2001 and Picco et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Inhibition of ETS1/2 gave only a weak down-regulation of Zic-r.b expression at the 32-cell stage.
claims.source: Inhibition of Fgf9/16/20, MEK or ETS1/2 (ETS1/2-MO) gave similar results, although inhibition of ETS1/2 gave only a weak down-regulation of Zic-r.b expression at the 32-cell stage, perhaps indicating the involvement of additional transcription factors that are also known to mediate FGF signals in Ciona embryos (Figure 2a; Table 1) (Bertrand et al., 2003; Gainous et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2a and Table 1, with inference about additional transcription factors supported by citations.

claims.claim: Maintenance of Foxa.a, Foxd and Fgf9/16/20 expression at the 32-cell stage is independent of each other.
claims.source: Maintenance of Foxa.a, Foxd and Fgf9/16/20 expression at the 32-cell stage is independent of each other (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a), as was shown previously for Foxd and Fgf9/16/20 in Ciona savigni embryos (Imai et al., 2002a).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and supported by citation to Imai et al., 2002a.

claims.claim: In FGF-inhibited embryos, Zic-r.b expression recovered at the 64-cell stage.
claims.source: In FGF-inhibited embryos, Zic-r.b expression recovered at the 64-cell stage (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a) (Imai et al., 2006; Kumano et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Zic-r.b expression at the 32- and 64-cell stages can be mediated by separate enhancer elements.
claims.source: Zic-r.b expression at the 32- and 64-cell stages can be mediated by separate enhancer elements (Anno et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Anno et al., 2006.

claims.claim: In the NN-cell lineage, FGF-signalling is required for notochord fate, but has to be attenuated for neural fate.
claims.source: In addition, in the NN-cell lineage, FGF-signalling is required for notochord fate, but has to be attenuated for neural fate (Minokawa et al, 2001; Picco et al., 2007; Yasuo and Hudson, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Minokawa et al., 2001, Picco et al., 2007, and Yasuo and Hudson, 2007.

claims.claim: In Foxa.a- and Foxd- inhibited embryos, Zic-r.b continues to be repressed in the NN-cell lineages at the 64-cell stage and later.
claims.source: In Foxa.a- and Foxd- inhibited embryos, Zic-r.b continues to be repressed in the NN-cell lineages at the 64-cell stage (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a) and later (Imai et al., 2006), consistent with a requirement for Foxa.a and Foxd for both NN cell lineage-derived structures, the notochord and caudal central nervous system (CNS) (Imai et al., 2002b, 2006).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Endoderm gene expression was continuously reduced up to at least the early gastrula stage, following inhibition of any one of the NNE factors.
claims.source: Endoderm gene expression was continuously reduced up to at least the early gastrula stage, following inhibition of any one of the NNE factors (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–e).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–e.

claims.claim: A complete loss of endoderm at larval stages was observed only in Foxa.a-inhibited embryos.
claims.source: However, using alkaline phosphatase activity as an indicator of endoderm formation (Whittaker, 1977), a complete loss of endoderm at larval stages was observed only in Foxa.a-inhibited embryos, consistent with previous studies (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) (Imai et al., 2002b, 2006).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and supported by citations.

claims.claim: In Foxd and FGF-signal inhibited embryos, a large domain of alkaline phosphatase activity could be detected, suggesting that endoderm fate recovers in these embryos.
claims.source: In Foxd and FGF-signal inhibited embryos, a large domain of alkaline phosphatase activity could be detected, suggesting that endoderm fate recovers in these embryos (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 with inference about fate recovery.

claims.claim: Simultaneous repression of Foxd and FGF-signalling resulted in both a stronger repression of early endoderm gene expression as well as an almost complete absence of alkaline phosphatase activity at larval stages.
claims.source: Simultaneous repression of Foxd and FGF-signalling, however, resulted in both a stronger repression of early endoderm gene expression as well as an almost complete absence of alkaline phosphatase activity at larval stages (Figure 2—figure supplement 1–2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1–2.

claims.claim: For eventual endoderm formation, the embryo is able to compensate for loss of either Foxd or FGF-signals but is not able to compensate for loss of both.
claims.source: Thus, for eventual endoderm formation, the embryo is able to compensate for loss of either Foxd or FGF-signals but is not able to compensate for loss of both.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data showing recovery of endoderm with single inhibitions but not double inhibition.

claims.claim: nβ-catenin represses the ectoderm gene programme in vegetal cells.
claims.source: As well as promoting vegetal 'mesendoderm' fates, nβ-catenin also represses the ectoderm gene programme in vegetal cells (Hudson et al., 2013; Imai et al., 2000; Oda-Ishii et al., 2016; Rothbächer et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: In β-catenin knock-down embryos, ectopic expression of the early ectoderm gene Efna.d is observed in both NN and E cells at the 32-cell stage.
claims.source: In β-catenin knock-down embryos, ectopic expression of the early ectoderm gene Efna.d (formally ephrin-Ad) is observed in both NN and E cells at the 32-cell stage (Figure 2b) (Hudson et al., 2013) as well as in NNE cells at the 16-cell stage (Oda-Ishii et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2b and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Double inhibition of Foxd and FGF-signals resulted in ectopic expression of Efna.d in NN cells, but never in E cells.
claims.source: Double inhibition of Foxd and FGF-signals also resulted in ectopic expression of Efna.d in NN cells, but never in E cells (Figure 2b).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2b.

claims.claim: NNE factors repress the ectoderm genetic programme in NN cells.
claims.source: Thus, NNE factors repress the ectoderm genetic programme in NN cells.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the observation that double inhibition of Foxd and FGF-signals leads to ectopic ectoderm gene expression in NN cells.

claims.claim: nβ-catenin can repress the ectoderm genetic programme both via and independently of the NNE factors.
claims.source: A lack of derepression in E cells is probably due to the presence of nβ-catenin in E cells at the 32-cell stage (Hudson et al., 2013), suggesting that nβ-catenin can repress the ectoderm genetic programme both via and independently of the NNE factors.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that E cells do not show ectopic ectoderm gene expression even when NNE factors are inhibited, combined with knowledge that E cells have active nβ-catenin.

claims.claim: Co-expression of Foxa.a, Foxd and Fgf9/16/20 takes place only in mesendoderm lineages, the NNE and B-line mesendoderm lineages of the 16- and 32-cell stage embryo.
claims.source: Indeed, co-expression of these three factors takes place only in mesendoderm lineages, the NNE and B-line mesendoderm lineages of the 16- and 32-cell stage embryo (Figure 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by expression data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claims.claim: At the 32-cell stage, the E cells continue to express Foxa.a, Foxd and Fgf9/16/20, while NN cells express only Foxa.a and Fgf9/16/20.
claims.source: At the 32-cell stage, the E cells continue to express these three genes, while NN cells express only Foxa.a and Fgf9/16/20.
claims.evidence: This is based on expression data from the manuscript.

claims.claim: Foxd transcripts preferentially segregate into the NN cells during the NN-E cell division, before they rapidly disappear.
claims.source: However, we have previously shown that Foxd transcripts preferentially segregate into the NN cells during the NN-E cell division, before they rapidly disappear (Hudson et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Hudson et al., 2013.

claims.claim: NN cells contain Foxd transcripts early in their cell cycle.
claims.source: Thus, NN cells also contain Foxd transcripts early in their cell cycle.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Foxd transcripts segregate into NN cells during division.

claims.claim: Foxa.a is expressed in a-line anterior animal cells.
claims.source: As well as in vegetal cells, Foxa.a is also expressed in a-line anterior animal cells and ERK1/2 is activated in one pair of a-line cells (the a6.5 pair) at the 32-cell stage (Figure 3a) (Hudson et al., 2003; Lamy et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figure 3a and supported by citations.

claims.claim: ERK1/2 is activated in one pair of a-line cells (the a6.5 pair) at the 32-cell stage.
claims.source: As well as in vegetal cells, Foxa.a is also expressed in a-line anterior animal cells and ERK1/2 is activated in one pair of a-line cells (the a6.5 pair) at the 32-cell stage (Figure 3a) (Hudson et al., 2003; Lamy et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figure 3a and supported by citations.

claims.claim: a6.5 cells possess two of the three mesendoderm lineage specifiers (Foxa.a and activated ERK) and yet they do not adopt an NNE-like lineage.
claims.source: Thus, a6.5 cells possess two of the three mesendoderm lineage specifiers and yet they do not adopt an NNE-like lineage.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the expression data and the observation that a6.5 cells remain ectodermal.

claims.claim: Reintroduction of Foxd by mRNA injection was able to convert a-line cells to a mesendoderm state.
claims.source: Consistent with the notion that coexpression of Foxa.a, Foxd and Fgf9/16/20 represents a NNE regulatory state, reintroduction of the remaining factor, Foxd, by mRNA injection, was able to convert a-line cells to a mesendoderm state (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Injection of Foxd mRNA resulted in ectopic expression of Zic-r.b in a-line cells at the 32-cell stage.
claims.source: Injection of Foxd mRNA resulted in ectopic expression of Zic-r.b in a-line cells at the 32-cell stage (Figure 3b) (Imai et al., 2002c).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3b and supported by citation.

claims.claim: Injection of Foxd mRNA induced expression of Bra, a marker of notochord precursors, at the 64-cell stage.
claims.source: Similarly, expression of Bra, a marker of notochord precursors, was induced at the 64-cell stage (Figure 3b).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3b.

claims.claim: Foxd mRNA injection led to weak activation of Fgf9/16/20 and strong inhibition of Efna.d expression in the ectoderm cells.
claims.source: The most likely reason for this was that Foxd mRNA injection led to weak activation of Fgf9/16/20 and strong inhibition of Efna.d expression in the ectoderm cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Efna.d is a known antagonist of FGF-signals in Ciona.
claims.source: Efna.d is a known antagonist of FGF-signals in Ciona and its inhibition results in widespread activation of ERK1/2 in ectoderm lineages (Ohta and Satou, 2013; Picco et al., 2007; Shi and Levine, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Ohta and Satou, 2013, Picco et al., 2007, and Shi and Levine, 2008.

claims.claim: Inhibition of Efna.d results in widespread activation of ERK1/2 in ectoderm lineages.
claims.source: Efna.d is a known antagonist of FGF-signals in Ciona and its inhibition results in widespread activation of ERK1/2 in ectoderm lineages (Ohta and Satou, 2013; Picco et al., 2007; Shi and Levine, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Ohta and Satou, 2013, Picco et al., 2007, and Shi and Levine, 2008.

claims.claim: When Foxd mRNA-injected embryos were treated with U0126, the ectopic expression of Zic-r.b was reduced and Bra expression was completely suppressed.
claims.source: Consistent with this, when Foxd mRNA-injected embryos were treated with U0126, the ectopic expression of Zic-r.b was reduced and Bra expression was completely suppressed, mimicking the effect of MEK inhibition on endogenous Zic-r.b and Bra gene expression (Figure 3b).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3b.

claims.claim: Injection of Foxd mRNA is sufficient to convert Foxa.a/ERK1/2-positive a-line cells into mesoderm.
claims.source: Thus, injection of Foxd mRNA is sufficient to convert Foxa.a/ERK1/2-positive a-line cells into mesoderm.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data showing induction of mesoderm markers in a-line cells upon Foxd mRNA injection.

claims.claim: Injection of Foxd mRNA was not sufficient to induce endoderm gene expression in ectoderm cells.
claims.source: Injection of Foxd mRNA, however, was not sufficient to induce endoderm gene expression in ectoderm cells (Figure 3c).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3c.

claims.claim: When Foxd-mRNA injected embryos were treated from the late 16-cell stage with BIO, both Zic-r.b and Bra were repressed and Lhx3/4 ectopically activated in the a-line ectoderm cells.
claims.source: Accordingly, when Foxd-mRNA injected embryos were treated from the late 16-cell stage with BIO in order to mimic the second input of nβ-catenin activation, both Zic-r.b and Bra were repressed and Lhx3/4 ectopically activated in the a-line ectoderm cells (Figure 3b–c).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3b–c.

claims.claim: The NNE-like state induced in animal cells by Foxd mRNA injection behaves in the same way as NNE state of unmanipulated embryos.
claims.source: Thus, the NNE-like state induced in animal cells by Foxd mRNA injection behaves in the same way as NNE state of unmanipulated embryos.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the observation that the ectopic NNE state responds to β-catenin activation by switching to endoderm fate, just like endogenous NNE cells.

claims.claim: Injection of Foxd mRNA was able to rescue expression of NN-lineage genes (Zic-r.b and Bra) in β-catenin-MO embryos.
claims.source: Consistent with this, injection of Foxd mRNA was able to rescue expression of NN-lineage genes (Zic-r.b and Bra) in β-catenin-MO embryos and, as expected, this recovery depended on an intact FGF-signalling pathway (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The rescue of NN-lineage genes by Foxd mRNA in β-catenin-MO embryos depended on an intact FGF-signalling pathway.
claims.source: Consistent with this, injection of Foxd mRNA was able to rescue expression of NN-lineage genes (Zic-r.b and Bra) in β-catenin-MO embryos and, as expected, this recovery depended on an intact FGF-signalling pathway (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Co-expression of Foxd+Foxa.a+Fgf9/16/20 is sufficient to induce a mesendoderm regulatory state, which can then be further programmed into mesoderm or endoderm lineage by manipulation of nβ-catenin activity.
claims.source: We conclude that co-expression of Foxd+Foxa.a+Fgf9/16/20 is sufficient to induce a mesendoderm regulatory state, which can then be further programmed into mesoderm or endoderm lineage by manipulation of nβ-catenin activity.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on the combined experimental evidence from Figures 3-4.

claims.claim: The upstream regulatory sequences of the Fucosyltransferase-like (FT) gene become active in ectoderm cells from the 64-cell stage.
claims.source: The upstream regulatory sequences of the Fucosyltransferase-like (FT) gene become active in ectoderm cells from the 64-cell stage, when the ectoderm genetic programme is already underway (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and when these cells no longer express Foxa.a, Foxd or Fgf9/16/20 (Imai et al., 2004; Pasini et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and supported by citations.

claims.claim: There is a clear combinatorial effect between Foxa.a, Foxd and Fgf9/16/20 on the reprogramming of ectoderm to mesoderm, with strong induction of Bra seen only when all three constructs were co-electroporated.
claims.source: We observed a clear combinatorial effect between Foxa.a, Foxd and Fgf9/16/20 on the reprogramming of ectoderm to mesoderm, with strong induction of Bra seen only when all three constructs were co-electroporated (Figure 5b).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 5b.

claims.claim: Reprogramming of ectoderm to mesoderm by Foxa.a, Foxd and Fgf9/16/20 was accompanied by a strong downregulation of ectoderm gene expression and ectopic expression of Zic-r.b in the ectoderm cells.
claims.source: This reprogramming was accompanied by a strong downregulation of ectoderm gene expression and ectopic expression of Zic-r.b in the ectoderm cells of whole embryos (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Ectoderm explants could be reprogrammed to adopt an endoderm state when electroporated with pFT>Foxa.a, pFT>Foxd and pFT>Fgf9/16/20 and treated with a pulse of BIO from the 76-cell stage.
claims.source: Furthermore, ectoderm explants could be reprogrammed to adopt an endoderm state (Figure 5c). To achieve this, ectoderm explants from embryos electroporated with the triple combination (pFT>Foxa.a, pFT>Foxd and pFT>Fgf9/16/20) were treated with a pulse of BIO from the 76-cell stage to mimic the second round of nβ-catenin activation that normally drives the segregation of NN and E lineages (Figure 5c).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 5c.

claims.claim: BIO-treatment was able to induce nuclear translocation of β-catenin in isolated explants at the 76-cell stage.
claims.source: We confirmed that BIO-treatment was able to induce nuclear translocation of β-catenin in isolated explants at the 76-cell stage (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Coupling Foxa.a, Foxd and Fgf9/16/20 with BIO-treatment resulted in strong induction of Lhx3/4 expression.
claims.source: Coupling these three factors with BIO-treatment resulted in strong induction of Lhx3/4 expression.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 5c.

claims.claim: Foxa.a and Foxd can bind to the upstream sequences of both Zic-r.b (NN lineage) and Lhx3/4 (E lineage), suggesting that this genetic interaction is direct.
claims.source: Similarly, Foxa.a and Foxd can bind to the upstream sequences of both Zic-r.b (NN lineage) and Lhx3/4 (E lineage), suggesting that this genetic interaction is direct (Kubo et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Kubo et al., 2010 with inference about direct interaction.

claims.claim: In sea urchins and anamniote vertebrates, mesendoderm has been described as a mixed regulatory state with simultaneous activation of mesoderm and endoderm GRNs, prior to the lineage segregation of these fates.
claims.source: For example, in sea urchins and anamniote vertebrates, mesendoderm has been described as a mixed regulatory state with simultaneous activation of mesoderm and endoderm GRNs, prior to the lineage segregation of these fates (Peter and Davidson, 2010; Rodaway and Patient, 2001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Peter and Davidson, 2010 and Rodaway and Patient, 2001.

claims.claim: In sea urchin and sea stars, genes interacting with both mesoderm and endoderm GRNs have been identified.
claims.source: In sea urchin and sea stars, for example, genes interacting with both mesoderm and endoderm GRNs have been identified (http://sugp.caltech.edu/endomes/) (Davidson et al., 2002; McCauley et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Davidson et al., 2002 and McCauley et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The β-catenin/TCF complex promotes endoderm or mesendoderm in a wide range of organisms, and this process is therefore likely to represent an ancestral mechanism.
claims.source: The β-catenin/TCF complex promotes endoderm or mesendoderm in a wide range of organisms, and this process is therefore likely to represent an ancestral mechanism (Darras et al., 2011; Henry et al., 2008; Hudson et al., 2013; Imai et al., 2000; Logan et al., 1999; McCauley et al., 2015; Miyawaki et al., 2003; Momose and Houliston, 2007; Wikramanayake et al., 1998, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and represents an inference about evolutionary conservation.

claims.claim: The earliest steps of germ layer segregation in ascidian embryos are mediated by two rounds of nuclear(n)-β−catenin-dependent binary fate decisions.
claims.source: We have previously shown that the earliest steps of germ layer segregation in ascidian embryos are mediated by two rounds of nuclear(n)-β−catenin-dependent binary fate decisions.
claims.evidence: This is stated as previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: The first nβ-catenin-driven binary fate decision takes place at the 8- to 16-cell stage.
claims.source: The first nβ-catenin-driven binary fate decision takes place at the 8- to 16-cell stage.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ascidian development.

claims.claim: During the first nβ-catenin-driven binary fate decision, the β-catenin/TCF complex is differentially activated between mesendoderm and ectoderm progenitors, resulting in segregation of these lineages.
claims.source: During this process, the β-catenin/TCF complex is differentially activated between mesendoderm and ectoderm progenitors, resulting in segregation of these lineages (Figure 1a) (Hudson et al., 2013; Oda-Ishii et al., 2016; Rothbächer et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1a and supported by citations.

claims.claim: The second nβ-catenin-driven binary fate decision takes place at the 32-cell stage and controls the segregation of NNE mesendoderm cells into endoderm (E cell) and notochord/neural (NN cell) lineages.
claims.source: The second step takes place at the 32-cell stage and controls the segregation of NNE mesendoderm cells into endoderm (E cell) and notochord/neural (NN cell) lineages (Hudson et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Hudson et al., 2013.

claims.claim: During the second nβ-catenin-driven binary fate decision, the β-catenin/TCF complex is differentially activated between E and NN cells.
claims.source: During this step, the β-catenin/TCF complex is again differentially activated between E and NN cells (Figure 1a).
claims.evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1a.

claims.claim: Cells in which nβ-catenin remains active during the two steps (ON + ON) are specified as endoderm lineage.
claims.source: Therefore, cells in which nβ-catenin remains active during the two steps (ON + ON) are specified as endoderm lineage, cells in which nβ-catenin remains inactive during the two steps (OFF + OFF) are specified as ectoderm lineage and cells in which nβ-catenin is active during the first step but inactive during the second step (ON + OFF) are specified as notochord-neural lineage (Hudson et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Hudson et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Cells in which nβ-catenin remains inactive during the two steps (OFF + OFF) are specified as ectoderm lineage.
claims.source: Therefore, cells in which nβ-catenin remains active during the two steps (ON + ON) are specified as endoderm lineage, cells in which nβ-catenin remains inactive during the two steps (OFF + OFF) are specified as ectoderm lineage and cells in which nβ-catenin is active during the first step but inactive during the second step (ON + OFF) are specified as notochord-neural lineage (Hudson et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Hudson et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Cells in which nβ-catenin is active during the first step but inactive during the second step (ON + OFF) are specified as notochord-neural lineage.
claims.source: Therefore, cells in which nβ-catenin remains active during the two steps (ON + ON) are specified as endoderm lineage, cells in which nβ-catenin remains inactive during the two steps (OFF + OFF) are specified as ectoderm lineage and cells in which nβ-catenin is active during the first step but inactive during the second step (ON + OFF) are specified as notochord-neural lineage (Hudson et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Hudson et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Two rounds of nβ-catenin-driven switches result in transcriptional activation of the lineage specifiers, Zic-related.b (Zic-r.b) and Lhx3/4, in NN and E cells, respectively.
claims.source: These two rounds of nβ-catenin-driven switches result in transcriptional activation of the lineage specifiers, Zic-related.b (Zic-r.b, formally ZicL) and Lhx3/4 (formally Lhx3), in NN and E cells, respectively (Imai et al., 2002c; Satou et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Imai et al., 2002c and Satou et al., 2001.

claims.claim: The transient regulatory state induced by the first nβ-catenin input in NNE cells confers a distinct transcriptional response to the second nβ-catenin input on E cells.
claims.source: Thus, in the NNE lineage, it is likely that the transient regulatory state induced by the first nβ-catenin input in NNE cells confers a distinct transcriptional response to the second nβ-catenin input on E cells.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the same nβ-catenin signal is interpreted differently at different stages.

claims.claim: At the 8- to 16-cell stage of development, nβ-catenin, activated specifically in vegetal cells by as yet unknown mechanisms, promotes Foxa.a, Foxd and Fgf9/16/20 expression and represses ectoderm gene expression.
claims.source: At the 8- to 16-cell stage of development, nβ-catenin, activated specifically in vegetal cells by as yet unknown mechanisms, promotes Foxa.a, Foxd and Fgf9/16/20 expression and represses ectoderm gene expression (Hudson et al., 2013; Imai et al., 2000; Oda-Ishii et al., 2016; Rothbächer et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: ERK1/2 activity is detected in both notochord and endoderm until the early gastrula stage.
claims.source: For example, ERK1/2 activity is detected in both notochord and endoderm until the early gastrula stage (Nishida, 2003; Yasuo and Hudson, 2007), Fgf9/16/20 is required at the 64-cell stage for induction of notochord and repression of neural gene expression in the notochord lineage (Imai et al., 2002a; Kim and Nishida, 2001; Minokawa et al., 2001; Yasuo and Hudson, 2007) and Foxa.a is continuously expressed in notochord and endoderm, suggesting an on-going role for Foxa.a in both of these lineages (Imai et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Nishida, 2003 and Yasuo and Hudson, 2007.

claims.claim: Fgf9/16/20 is required at the 64-cell stage for induction of notochord and repression of neural gene expression in the notochord lineage.
claims.source: For example, ERK1/2 activity is detected in both notochord and endoderm until the early gastrula stage (Nishida, 2003; Yasuo and Hudson, 2007), Fgf9/16/20 is required at the 64-cell stage for induction of notochord and repression of neural gene expression in the notochord lineage (Imai et al., 2002a; Kim and Nishida, 2001; Minokawa et al., 2001; Yasuo and Hudson, 2007) and Foxa.a is continuously expressed in notochord and endoderm, suggesting an on-going role for Foxa.a in both of these lineages (Imai et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Imai et al., 2002a, Kim and Nishida, 2001, Minokawa et al., 2001, and Yasuo and Hudson, 2007.

claims.claim: Foxa.a is continuously expressed in notochord and endoderm, suggesting an on-going role for Foxa.a in both of these lineages.
claims.source: For example, ERK1/2 activity is detected in both notochord and endoderm until the early gastrula stage (Nishida, 2003; Yasuo and Hudson, 2007), Fgf9/16/20 is required at the 64-cell stage for induction of notochord and repression of neural gene expression in the notochord lineage (Imai et al., 2002a; Kim and Nishida, 2001; Minokawa et al., 2001; Yasuo and Hudson, 2007) and Foxa.a is continuously expressed in notochord and endoderm, suggesting an on-going role for Foxa.a in both of these lineages (Imai et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Imai et al., 2004 with inference about ongoing role.

claims.claim: The NN cell generates the posterior part of the CNS, including the equivalent of the 'spinal cord' of vertebrates.
claims.source: In addition to notochord, the NN cell generates the posterior part of the CNS, including the equivalent of the 'spinal cord' of vertebrates (reviewed in [Hudson, 2016]).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a review by Hudson, 2016.

claims.claim: The binary cell fate decision between neural and notochord takes place at the 64-cell stage.
claims.source: The binary cell fate decision between neural and notochord takes place at the 64-cell stage (Minokawa et al., 2001; Picco et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Minokawa et al., 2001 and Picco et al., 2007.

claims.claim: The lateral neural progenitors that arise from the NN-cell lineage produce a muscle cell during neural plate patterning, following another neuromesodermal binary fate decision.
claims.source: The lateral neural progenitors that arise from the NN-cell lineage also produce a muscle cell during neural plate patterning, following another neuromesodermal binary fate decision (reviewed in [Hudson and Yasuo, 2008]).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a review by Hudson and Yasuo, 2008.

claims.claim: In the zebrafish tailbud, bipotential neuromesodermal progenitor cells generate notochord and floorplate (ventral spinal cord).
claims.source: For example, in the zebrafish tailbud, bipotential neuromesodermal progenitor cells generate notochord and floorplate (ventral spinal cord) (Row et al., 2016) and in both human and mouse embryonic stem cells and zebrafish tailbud stem cells, bipotential neuromesodermal progenitors generate paraxial mesoderm and posterior neural tube (Gouti et al., 2014; Martin and Kimelman, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Row et al., 2016.

claims.claim: In both human and mouse embryonic stem cells and zebrafish tailbud stem cells, bipotential neuromesodermal progenitors generate paraxial mesoderm and posterior neural tube.
claims.source: For example, in the zebrafish tailbud, bipotential neuromesodermal progenitor cells generate notochord and floorplate (ventral spinal cord) (Row et al., 2016) and in both human and mouse embryonic stem cells and zebrafish tailbud stem cells, bipotential neuromesodermal progenitors generate paraxial mesoderm and posterior neural tube (Gouti et al., 2014; Martin and Kimelman, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Gouti et al., 2014 and Martin and Kimelman, 2012.

claims.claim: In the C. elegans EMS cell, the MS (mesoderm) lineage also gives rise to some neurons.
claims.source: Even in the classical mesendoderm model, that is the C. elegans EMS cell, the MS (mesoderm) lineage also gives rise to some neurons (Sulston and Horvitz, 1977; Sulston et al., 1983).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Sulston and Horvitz, 1977 and Sulston et al., 1983.

claims.claim: At the 64-cell stage, the lateral E cell divides into one endoderm and one trunk lateral cell (mesenchyme) precursor, following induction of trunk lateral cell fate.
claims.source: At the 64-cell stage of development, the lateral E cell divides into one endoderm and one trunk lateral cell (mesenchyme) precursor, following induction of trunk lateral cell fate (Shi and Levine, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Shi and Levine, 2008.

claims.claim: In the C. elegans EMS cell, the MED1/2 GATA factors feed into both E (endoderm) and MS (mesoderm) lineage specification, such that MED1/2 directly activates both MS and E target genes.
claims.source: The mesendoderm regulatory state in ascidian embryos is similar to the situation in the C. elegans EMS cell in which the MED1/2 GATA factors feed into both E (endoderm) and MS (mesoderm) lineage specification, such that MED1/2 directly activates both MS and E target genes (Broitman-Maduro et al., 2005; Maduro et al., 2001, 2015; McGhee, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Broitman-Maduro et al., 2005, Maduro et al., 2001, 2015, and McGhee, 2013.

claims.claim: β-catenin can repress ectoderm gene expression via a physical interaction between β-catenin/Tcf7 and Gata.a, preventing this key regulator of ectoderm lineage from binding to its DNA target sites.
claims.source: Recently, it has been shown that this can take place via a physical interaction between β-catenin/Tcf7 and Gata.a, preventing this key regulator of ectoderm lineage from binding to its DNA target sites (Oda-Ishii et al., 2016; Rothbächer et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Oda-Ishii et al., 2016 and Rothbächer et al., 2007.

results.result: Foxa.a, Foxd, and Fgf9/16/20 are transcriptional targets of nβ-catenin in vegetal cells at the 16-cell stage. Loss-of-function experiments show that β-catenin inhibition eliminates Foxd and Fgf9/16/20 expression, while gain-of-function experiments with BIO treatment induce all three genes in ectoderm lineages.
results.evaluation: Claims C14, C17, and C18 are well-supported by experimental data in Figure 1b-c showing loss of Foxd/Fgf9/16/20 expression upon β-catenin inhibition and ectopic activation upon β-catenin stabilization. The data are consistent with prior work (C13) and provide clear evidence for β-catenin-dependent regulation of these factors.

results.result: Each of the three factors (Foxa.a, Foxd, and Fgf9/16/20) is individually required for correct initiation of both NN (Zic-r.b) and E (Lhx3/4) lineage gene expression at the 32-cell stage. Fgf9/16/20 activates ERK in vegetal lineages, and inhibition of any single factor disrupts both mesoderm and endoderm marker expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C22, C23, C25, and C26 are strongly supported by experimental data in Figure 2a, Table 1, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1. Morpholino knockdown of each factor individually prevents proper initiation of both NN and E lineage markers, demonstrating their requirement for both lineages. The independence of their maintenance (C26) is also experimentally validated.

results.result: Endoderm gene expression is continuously reduced following inhibition of any NNE factor through early gastrula stage. However, only Foxa.a inhibition causes complete loss of endoderm at larval stages, while Foxd or FGF-signal inhibition alone allows endoderm recovery. Double inhibition of Foxd and FGF-signaling prevents endoderm recovery, indicating redundancy between these two factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C35 are supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1-2 showing temporal gene expression patterns and alkaline phosphatase activity. The compensatory mechanism between Foxd and FGF-signaling is demonstrated by single versus double inhibition experiments, though the molecular basis for this compensation is not explored.

results.result: NNE factors (Foxd and FGF-signals) repress the ectoderm genetic program in NN cells, as double inhibition causes ectopic ectoderm gene (Efna.d) expression in NN but not E cells. The lack of derepression in E cells suggests nβ-catenin can repress ectoderm genes both via and independently of NNE factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40 are supported by experimental data in Figure 2b showing cell-type-specific ectopic Efna.d expression. The inference about dual mechanisms of ectoderm repression (C40) is reasonable given the differential response of NN versus E cells, though direct mechanistic evidence is limited to prior citations (C94).

results.result: Co-expression of Foxa.a, Foxd, and Fgf9/16/20 occurs exclusively in mesendoderm lineages (NNE and B-line) at 16- and 32-cell stages. At 32-cell stage, E cells continue expressing all three genes while NN cells express only Foxa.a and Fgf9/16/20, though Foxd transcripts transiently segregate into NN cells during division.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C44 are supported by expression data in Figures 1 and 2—figure supplement 1a, combined with prior work (C43). The transient presence of Foxd in NN cells is inferred from previous observations of transcript segregation, making the co-expression window brief but present in both lineages.

results.result: Injection of Foxd mRNA into embryos converts a-line ectoderm cells (which already express Foxa.a and have ERK activation) to a mesendoderm state, inducing ectopic expression of mesoderm markers Zic-r.b and Bra. This conversion depends on FGF signaling, as MEK inhibition suppresses the ectopic mesoderm markers.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C55 are well-supported by experimental data in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1. The sufficiency of Foxd to convert Foxa.a/ERK-positive cells to mesoderm is clearly demonstrated, and the FGF-dependence is confirmed by U0126 treatment. The mechanism involves Foxd-mediated activation of Fgf9/16/20 and repression of Efna.d (C51).

results.result: Foxd mRNA injection alone is insufficient to induce endoderm gene expression in ectoderm cells. However, when combined with BIO treatment (mimicking the second nβ-catenin activation), the ectopic NNE-like state switches to endoderm fate, with repression of mesoderm markers (Zic-r.b, Bra) and activation of endoderm marker (Lhx3/4).
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58 are supported by data in Figure 3b-c showing that the ectopic mesendoderm state responds to β-catenin modulation similarly to endogenous NNE cells. This demonstrates that the induced state is functionally equivalent to the natural mesendoderm state and can be programmed by the second β-catenin signal.

results.result: Foxd mRNA injection rescues NN-lineage gene expression (Zic-r.b and Bra) in β-catenin-knockdown embryos in an FGF-signaling-dependent manner. This demonstrates that co-expression of Foxd, Foxa.a, and Fgf9/16/20 is sufficient to induce a mesendoderm regulatory state that can be programmed into mesoderm or endoderm by modulating nβ-catenin activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C61 are supported by rescue experiments in Figure 4. The ability of Foxd to rescue mesoderm markers in β-catenin-deficient embryos (which retain Foxa.a expression) provides strong evidence for sufficiency of the three-factor combination, though the rescue is partial and FGF-dependent.

results.result: Ectopic co-expression of all three factors (Foxa.a, Foxd, and Fgf9/16/20) using FT promoter-driven constructs in isolated ectoderm explants is sufficient to reprogramme ectoderm to mesendoderm. Strong Bra induction occurs only with all three factors together, accompanied by downregulation of ectoderm genes. Addition of BIO treatment converts the reprogrammed state to endoderm (Lhx3/4 expression).
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C63-C65, and C67 are strongly supported by reprogramming experiments in Figure 5 using isolated ectoderm explants. The combinatorial requirement is clearly demonstrated, and the ability to direct the induced state toward either mesoderm or endoderm by β-catenin modulation validates the mesendoderm ground state model. The use of isolated explants eliminates confounding signals from vegetal cells.

results.result: The transient mesendoderm regulatory state in ascidian embryos is defined by co-expression of Foxa.a, Foxd, and Fgf9/16/20. This state is both necessary (each factor required for both lineages) and sufficient (can reprogram ectoderm) for mesendoderm specification, and can be programmed into mesoderm or endoderm by differential nβ-catenin activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C5 and C61 represent the main conclusions of the manuscript, synthesizing the necessity data (Figure 2), sufficiency in endogenous context (Figures 3-4), and reprogramming experiments (Figure 5). The evidence collectively supports this model, though some aspects (like the precise molecular mechanisms of lineage choice) remain to be elucidated.

results.result: BIO treatment induces nuclear translocation of β-catenin in isolated ectoderm explants at the 76-cell stage, confirming that the chemical treatment effectively activates the β-catenin pathway in the experimental system.
results.evaluation: Claim C66 is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 showing nuclear β-catenin in BIO-treated explants. This control experiment validates the experimental approach for mimicking the second nβ-catenin activation in isolated explants.

results.result: The manuscript describes the established lineage relationships in ascidian embryos: the first A-V division segregates mesendoderm (A- and B-line) from ectoderm (a- and b-line) at 8-cell stage; A4.1 blastomeres generate NNE cells at 16-cell stage; NNE cells divide to produce NN and E cells at 32-cell stage; NN cells segregate into notochord and neural at 64-cell stage; E cells generate endoderm and some mesoderm; and neural plate generates muscle precursors.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C12 describe established developmental biology of ascidian embryos, supported by classical literature citations (Conklin 1905, Nishida 1987, Shi and Levine 2008, etc.) and illustrated in Figure 1a. These provide essential context for the experimental work but are not novel findings of this study.

results.result: Germ layer segregation in ascidian embryos occurs through two sequential nβ-catenin-driven binary fate decisions: the first (8-16 cell stage) segregates mesendoderm (ON) from ectoderm (OFF); the second (32-cell stage) segregates endoderm (ON+ON) from notochord-neural (ON+OFF). These switches activate lineage-specific transcription factors Zic-r.b (NN) and Lhx3/4 (E).
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C80 describe the two-step β-catenin model established in prior work by the authors (Hudson et al. 2013) and others, illustrated in Figure 1a. This model provides the conceptual framework for the current study but represents previously published work rather than new findings.

results.result: The mesendoderm regulatory architecture in ascidians is similar to C. elegans, where individual factors (Foxa.a/Foxd in ascidians; MED1/2 in C. elegans) directly activate both mesoderm and endoderm target genes. Foxa.a and Foxd can bind upstream sequences of both Zic-r.b (NN) and Lhx3/4 (E), suggesting direct regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C68 and C93 are supported by prior work (Kubo et al. 2010 for ascidians; multiple citations for C. elegans). The comparison provides important evolutionary context, though the directness of regulation in ascidians is inferred from binding data rather than demonstrated functionally in this study.

results.result: Nuclear β-catenin promotes mesendoderm over ectoderm lineages in many bilaterian embryos, representing a likely ancestral developmental mechanism conserved across diverse organisms including ascidians, sea urchins, vertebrates, and cnidarians.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C71 describe well-established general principles supported by extensive literature (multiple citations in C71). These provide important evolutionary context but represent prior knowledge rather than findings of this study.

results.result: In sea urchins and anamniote vertebrates, mesendoderm is described as a 'mixed regulatory state' with simultaneous activation of mesoderm and endoderm GRNs prior to lineage segregation. Some genes interacting with both GRNs have been identified in echinoderms.
results.evaluation: Claims C69 and C70 describe alternative mesendoderm regulatory architectures in other organisms, supported by citations. This comparison is used to distinguish the ascidian/nematode model (with obligate mesendoderm lineage specifiers) from the 'mixed-lineage' model, providing important conceptual context.

results.result: Foxa.a has both β-catenin-dependent expression in vegetal mesendoderm lineages and β-catenin-independent expression in a-line anterior ectoderm. In β-catenin-inhibited embryos, Foxa.a expression persists in NNE and a-lineage cells, likely due to transformation of vegetal cells to animal cell identity.
results.evaluation: Claims C13, C15, and C16 are supported by data in Figure 1b-c and prior work. The dual regulation of Foxa.a is important for interpreting the rescue experiments (where Foxa.a is present even in β-catenin knockdown embryos), though the inference about cell transformation (C16) is based on prior observations.

results.result: Prior work showed that Foxa.a is required for both NN and endoderm lineages, Foxd specifically for NN lineage but not endoderm, and Fgf9/16/20 contributes to notochord induction from NN lineage. The current study revises this understanding by showing all three factors are required for both lineages.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C21 describe prior understanding from cited work (Imai et al. 2002a,b, 2006; Yasuo and Hudson 2007). The current study's finding that all three factors are required for both lineages (C2, C22) represents a significant revision of this prior model, highlighting the novelty of the current findings.

results.result: Zic-r.b expression recovers at 64-cell stage in FGF-inhibited embryos but remains repressed in Foxa.a/Foxd-inhibited embryos. The 32- and 64-cell stage expression can be mediated by separate enhancers. FGF signaling is required for notochord but must be attenuated for neural fate in the NN lineage.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C30 are supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and prior work. These observations explain the temporal dynamics of gene expression and the differential requirements for FGF signaling in notochord versus neural fates, providing important mechanistic details.

results.result: In a-line ectoderm cells, Foxa.a is expressed and ERK1/2 is activated in the a6.5 pair at 32-cell stage. Despite possessing two of three mesendoderm specifiers (Foxa.a and activated ERK), these cells do not adopt NNE-like lineage, demonstrating that all three factors are required.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C47 are supported by expression data in Figure 3a and prior work. This natural experiment demonstrates the necessity of all three factors for mesendoderm specification and provides the rationale for the Foxd mRNA injection experiments.

results.result: Efna.d is a known antagonist of FGF signals in Ciona, and its inhibition results in widespread ERK1/2 activation in ectoderm lineages. This explains how Foxd overexpression (which represses Efna.d) leads to broad ERK activation and mesoderm marker induction.
results.evaluation: Claims C52 and C53 describe established knowledge from prior work (Ohta and Satou 2013; Picco et al. 2007; Shi and Levine 2008) that explains the mechanism underlying the Foxd overexpression phenotype (C51). This provides important mechanistic context for interpreting the gain-of-function experiments.

results.result: The Fucosyltransferase-like (FT) gene promoter becomes active in ectoderm cells from the 64-cell stage, when the ectoderm genetic program is already underway and these cells no longer express the three mesendoderm factors.
results.evaluation: Claim C62 is supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and prior work (Imai et al. 2004; Pasini et al. 2012). This timing is crucial for the reprogramming experiments, as it ensures the ectoderm cells are already committed when the ectopic factors are expressed.

results.result: The transient regulatory state induced by the first nβ-catenin input in NNE cells likely confers a distinct transcriptional response to the second nβ-catenin input in E cells. At 8-16 cell stage, nβ-catenin promotes Foxa.a, Foxd, and Fgf9/16/20 expression and represses ectoderm genes in vegetal cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C81 and C82 represent key conceptual points about how the same signal (nβ-catenin) is interpreted differently at different stages. C81 is an inference from the overall model, while C82 is supported by prior work. These claims articulate the central hypothesis that motivated the study.

results.result: The three mesendoderm factors have ongoing roles beyond initial specification: ERK1/2 activity persists in notochord and endoderm until early gastrula; Fgf9/16/20 is required at 64-cell stage for notochord induction and neural repression; Foxa.a is continuously expressed in both lineages.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C85 are supported by prior work (multiple citations) and suggest that these factors function not only in initial specification but also in subsequent lineage maintenance and differentiation. This provides important context for interpreting the persistent phenotypes observed in loss-of-function experiments.

results.result: The manuscript discusses bipotential progenitors in various systems: NN cells generate both notochord and neural tissue in ascidians; similar neuromesodermal progenitors exist in zebrafish, mouse, and human; even the C. elegans MS lineage produces some neurons; and ascidian E cells generate both endoderm and mesenchyme.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C92 provide comparative developmental biology context, supported by extensive citations. These comparisons emphasize that germ layer segregation is a progressive process across animals and that the ascidian NNE cell fits within a broader pattern of bipotential progenitors.

results.result: Nuclear β-catenin represses the ectoderm gene program in vegetal cells. In β-catenin knockdown embryos, ectopic ectoderm gene (Efna.d) expression occurs in both NN and E cells. This repression can occur via physical interaction between β-catenin/Tcf7 and Gata.a, preventing Gata.a from binding DNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C36, C37, and C94 are supported by data in Figure 2b and prior work (Hudson et al. 2013; Oda-Ishii et al. 2016; Rothbächer et al. 2007). The molecular mechanism (C94) is from recent prior work and provides important context for understanding how β-catenin promotes mesendoderm fate.
